title: Faith and Science
lead: How Jews and Christians have read the Bible alongside the study of nature, from the rabbis and Augustine to Galileo and today. The main traditions agree that God's word and God's world cannot finally disagree. They differ over what to do when the two seem to clash. The days of Genesis 1 and the age of the earth have their own page (The Days of Creation and the Age of the Earth).

sections.b:
The Bible praises God from both of his "books." "The heavens keep recounting God's glory" (Psalm 19:1), and "The LORD's law is flawless" (Psalm 19:7). Proverbs adds that "the glory of kings is searching a matter out" (Proverbs 25:2). The rabbis were ready to learn about nature from outsiders. The sages of Israel and of the nations disagreed about the sun's path at night. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi judged that the nations' sages were "more accurate than our statement." He reasoned from springs that are warmer at night (Talmud, Pesachim 94b).

Augustine warned Christians not to make the Bible say foolish things about nature. He wrote in Latin, in The Literal Meaning of Genesis (1.19.39). Even a non-Christian, he said, may know about the earth and sky, the stars, eclipses, animals and plants "by sure reasoning or experience." It is "very shameful and harmful" when such a person hears a Christian talk nonsense about these things as if from Scripture. If unbelievers catch Christians in errors about things they can test, how will they believe the Bible about the resurrection of the dead, eternal life and the kingdom of heaven?

Calvin made a related but different point. He said Genesis 1 speaks of the world as everyone sees it: "Moses wrote in a popular style things which without instruction, all ordinary persons, endued with common sense, are able to understand." Astronomers study what lies deeper, and their study "is not to be reprobated." Christian thinkers call this God's accommodation: God speaks in terms that people of the time could grasp.

In the early 1600s Galileo argued that the earth moves around the sun. A fixed earth seemed to fit a literal reading of verses such as Psalm 93:1, Psalm 104:5 and Ecclesiastes 1:5. In 1614 the friar Tommaso Caccini preached against Galileo's views on Joshua 10, where the sun stands still (see The Sun Stands Still).

In his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), Galileo replied that "two truths cannot contradict one another." He repeated a saying he had heard from a churchman of the highest rank. The Holy Spirit means "to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes." In 1616 the Inquisition declared the sun-centered view both scientifically indefensible and heretical. In 1633 it tried Galileo, found him "vehemently suspect of heresy," and placed him under house arrest.

The Catholic Church later revisited the case. Leo XIII taught in 1893 that "There can never, indeed, be any real discrepancy between the theologian and the physicist, as long as each confines himself within his own lines." The Bible's writers, he said, "described and dealt with things in more or less figurative language, or in terms which were commonly used at the time" (Providentissimus Deus 18). In 1992 John Paul II received the report of a commission set up in 1981. Speaking in French, he said that most theologians of Galileo's day "did not see the formal distinction between Holy Scripture and its interpretation." Galileo, "a sincere believer," saw this more clearly than his opponents. A "tragic mutual misunderstanding," the pope said, had been taken as proof that science and faith are enemies by nature.

The Catechism (159) quotes the First Vatican Council: "nor can truth ever contradict truth." It then quotes the Second Vatican Council: "methodical research in all branches of knowledge, provided it is carried out in a truly scientific manner and does not override moral laws, can never conflict with the faith, because the things of the world and the things of faith derive from the same God."

What scientists hold. The scientific consensus dates the earth to about 4.54 billion years, mainly from radiometric dating. Nearly all scientists also accept that living things have evolved over time; a 2009 Pew poll found 97%. Young-earth creationists dissent from both. Christians who accept the Bible as God's word answer in the ways below, each in its own words.

Scripture as the measure. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978, Article XII) denies that the Bible's truth is limited to spiritual themes "exclusive of assertions in the fields of history and science." It also denies "that scientific hypotheses about earth history may properly be used to overturn the teaching of Scripture on creation and the flood." Article XIII allows for "observational descriptions of nature."

Young-earth creation. Answers in Genesis holds that the Bible's authority "includes its assertions in such fields as history and science." It states, "No apparent, perceived, or claimed evidence in any field of study, including science, history, and chronology, can be valid if it contradicts the clear teaching of Scripture obtained by historical-grammatical interpretation." It gives the reason: "evidence is always subject to interpretation by fallible people who do not possess all information." Henry Morris, co-author of The Genesis Flood (1961), wrote, "The Bible is a book of science!"

Old-earth creation. Hugh Ross of Reasons to Believe, a leading progressive creationist, also looks for close agreement between Genesis and modern science. He wrote that no author "more than 3400 years ago" could "have so accurately described and sequenced these events" of Genesis 1 "without divine assistance." Denis Lamoureux calls this approach, which Morris and Ross share in different forms, "concordism."

Evolutionary creation. Lamoureux himself holds that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit created life "through an ordained and sustained evolutionary process." He reads the Bible's picture of the sky as the "ancient science" of its day. He separates it from "the inerrant message of faith."

Earlier voices. The Reformed theologian B. B. Warfield allowed that an inspired writer might "share the ordinary opinions of his day" about "the form of the earth, or its relation to the sun" (quoted by Paul Seely). Luther urged believing what Scripture says of "the waters above the heavens" even when it is beyond us. Catholic teaching, as above, holds that a true finding of science and the true sense of Scripture cannot clash. Jewish views on the age of the world are set out under The Days of Creation and the Age of the Earth.

On this site the Bible is taken as true, and science as the study of the world God made. Where the two seem to disagree, each view is set out with its reasons, without ranking them.

common: Science and Christianity have always been at war; historians trace this picture largely to nineteenth-century writers such as John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White.
The church taught a flat earth until Columbus.
uncommon: Augustine warned in the early 400s that Christians who talk nonsense about nature make unbelievers doubt what the Bible says about the resurrection.
In the Talmud, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi judged that non-Jewish sages were more accurate than the rabbis about the sun's path at night.
